UI-VALUE CALL, reading (a): add `native-mobile` (Expo app; conventions/native-mobile.md applies) and `native-desktop` (Tauri app; conventions/native-desktop.md applies). Keep `desktop-only` and sharpen its gloss to 'a local operator viewer served to a browser on 127.0.0.1 - not a shipped binary; a shipped desktop app is native-desktop'. Rename rejected: no script consumes `ui` (grep of .graph/, hooks, fleetview finds none), so a rename buys nothing and churns 2 registry entries plus 4 prose sites. MULTI-TARGET CALL: `ui` stays a string for single-surface apps and MAY be an array when ONE repo ships to several surfaces, e.g. ["responsive-web","native-mobile"]. Every new gate is worded 'when the app's ui includes X' (a string trivially includes itself), and each convention applies only to the code for its own surface. Expo+Tauri in one repo is legal but not the default: new-app recommends two apps (two repos) unless they are one product sharing one identity and release cadence - and a task spanning two repos remains two tasks. NEW FACT the scout did not record (flagged, not contradicting it): huntstack already ships an Expo app at huntstack/apps/mobile (app.json present; CURRENT-STATE.md:1000 run 2026-09-01-huntstack-mobile) while its registry ui is `responsive-web`. s1.$comment: RE-REVIEWS NEST, and this is the rule every reader follows. The TOP LEVEL of reviews.<slice> IS attempt 1. A re-review writes attempt_2, then attempt_3, and so on, each with the same fields as the top level. Every attempt SURVIVES PERMANENTLY - history is never overwritten, flattened, or migrated up. The LATEST attempt supplies the verdict: that is what close-run.py, brief.py and verify-state.py resolve through, and what fleetview's finalVerdict() has always shown. `ever_rejected` - did ANY attempt REJECT - is DISPLAY ONLY, forever, so a rejection stays visible after it is fixed; it must never gate anything, or the fleet stops being able to loop. NO NODE MAY REWRITE AN EARLIER ATTEMPT: a second reviewer writes its own attempt_N and leaves the ones before it alone, top-level verdict included - relocating that verdict would destroy the history the board keeps and leave a key stamped written_by:reviewer with someone else as its real author. The KEY INDEX numbers an attempt, not the `attempt` field inside it; the field is display. An EMPTY attempt_N is not a re-review, it is a key nobody wrote - write the whole attempt or none of it. The walk STOPS AT THE FIRST GAP, so an attempt_3 with no attempt_2 is ignored and the earlier verdict stands: A GAP IS MALFORMED AND NO NODE MAY LEAVE ONE. Write the next UNUSED N and never skip - a mis-numbered re-review is not reported anywhere, it is simply unread, and a REJECT nobody reads is a REJECT nobody acts on. The cap is attempt_9, matching fleetview's `for (i = 2; i < 10; i++)` exactly so the two readers cannot disagree; attempt_10 and beyond is reported loudly and resolved by nobody.
s1.summary: REJECT, one blocker. Re-ran done_when myself: OK, exit 0. Read all five diff files and the untracked registry.json: it is valid JSON, 141 lines (same as CURRENT-STATE's count), huntstack ui is ["responsive-web","native-mobile"] (approved at the gate), and the $comment matches the desktop-only gloss in mobile-first.md and native-desktop.md. There is no baseline to byte-compare the other entries against. Commit 63f3bfe: author and committer are njcurtis3, no Claude trailers. Read for technical accuracy: secrets go only in expo-secure-store, ios/ and android/ stay uncommitted, CSP is never null and has no unsafe-eval, fs and shell scopes are narrow, the updater pubkey is in config and the private key only in CI, the 44pt/48dp numbers are correct, and no step builds iOS on Windows. All of those point the right way. The blocker: native-mobile.md allows runtimeVersion policy appVersion but never says a native change must bump `version`. eas.json autoIncrement only raises buildNumber/versionCode. So the next eas update reaches old binaries that don't have the new native module, and checklist item 7 still passes. Notes are in findings.

findings.issue: runtimeVersion/OTA rule is incomplete for the appVersion policy it approves. Lines 73-78 allow `appVersion` and say a native change needs a new build, but only fingerprint changes the runtime version 'by itself'. Nothing says that under appVersion the app's `version` MUST be bumped. eas.json `autoIncrement` (line 28) raises buildNumber/versionCode, not `version`. Concrete failure: an app on runtimeVersion {policy:'appVersion'} at version 1.0.0 adds a native module and ships a new build with autoIncrement. runtimeVersion is still '1.0.0'. The next `eas update --channel production` goes to the old 1.0.0 binaries too, and their JS calls a native module that isn't there, so the app crashes or rolls back. Checklist item 7 ('shipped as a new build, runtimeVersion set with a policy') answers yes. Fix: either make fingerprint the default and require a stated reason for appVersion, or add the rule 'with appVersion, every native change bumps `version`' to the rules, to Prohibitions and to checklist item 7.

'The OS decides the webview version; the app cannot bundle its own' is wrong on Windows. Tauri 2 can ship a fixed WebView2 runtime (bundle.windows.webviewInstallMode: fixedRuntime). The statement holds for WKWebView and WebKitGTK. Reword it to: macOS and Linux use the OS webview, and Windows uses the evergreen WebView2 unless the app ships a fixed runtime.
'EAS secrets': EAS has replaced `eas secret:*` with EAS environment variables (visibility: secret/sensitive). Name the current mechanism so builders don't reach for a deprecated CLI.

The section header promises each prohibition is visible in a diff. 'No native change shipped as an OTA update' is only visible when the publish step is in a committed CI workflow. A manual `eas update` never shows up in a diff. Either say so or tie the prohibition to the workflow file.
'reviewer.md points here by name' (same line in native-desktop.md:103) is a forward reference. It only becomes true when s2 lands, so s2's review should confirm it does.

The updater section omits bundle.createUpdaterArtifacts: true, without which Tauri 2 produces no signed updater artifacts. connect-src guidance (line 45) could mention that Tauri 2 IPC uses ipc:/http://ipc.localhost. Neither is wrong as written, but both are easy to miss when copying the convention.
'Keep >= 8 between adjacent targets' has no unit (8pt/8dp).

In tauri.conf.json the value is an object, `{"type": "fixedRuntime", "path": "./<runtime-dir>/"}`, and the fixed runtime adds roughly 180MB to the installer. Writing the object form would stop a copier from pasting a bare string that fails schema validation. The prose is correct as written.

findings.detail: Tauri's updater only installs when the remote version is greater than the installed one (default comparator), so publishing latest.json pointing at the prior version halts spread but does not move clients already on the bad version back; the manifest itself is not signed, the artifacts are. 'installed binaries are not recalled' covers it, but the stronger roll-forward is re-releasing the prior code under a higher version. Worth a word if this line is touched again; not a wrong instruction.

findings.title: Malformed package.json is reported as both expo and tauri
findings.detail: _dir_native appends 'package.json unparseable' to both kinds, so any plain web app whose package.json (at depth <= 2, e.g. a deliberately broken test fixture) fails to parse yields an expo hit AND a tauri hit, and app_facts then emits two contradictions ('expo detected ... lacks native-mobile', 'tauri detected ...'). This is what the intent literally specifies, so not a builder miss; a separate 'unparseable' kind or excluding unparseable-only hits from contradictions_for would avoid the false alarm.

findings.title: --all output is not ASCII, pre-existing
findings.detail: Line 'RULE: Never commit the Roam export ...' carries a non-ASCII dash from registry.json; master's scout-facts.py produces the same byte. Not introduced here. New strings are ASCII, but dependency version strings and directory names are printed verbatim, so ASCII holds only as far as the inputs are.
